name: Volcanic ash

lead: Ground volcanic ash and related volcanic minerals appear in some Korean-origin masks and cleansers as oil-absorbing ingredients. People with oily skin use them for less shine, cleaner-feeling pores and a matte, clearer look.

The chain is absorption: the fine mineral particles take up surface sebum, so skin looks less shiny and pores look less clogged. Users and marketing describe this effect; no study of cosmetic volcanic ash on human skin was identified, and the literature found covers volcanology and exposure hazards.

paras: Used as a wash-off mask or cleanser, typically applied to the oily zones for several minutes once or twice a week, then rinsed and followed by moisturiser. It is often combined with other clay or charcoal products. Matte results are visible right after rinsing.
Raw eruption ash is abrasive and can irritate eyes, skin and airways. Cosmetic safety data were not found, and drying or over-cleansing can irritate skin.

angle.text: Volcanic ash appears in some K-beauty masks and cleansers, used to absorb oil and leave oily skin looking matte. The fine mineral particles take up surface sebum, which means less shine and cleaner-looking pores.

lead: Volcanic ash is fine fragmented rock, mineral crystal and volcanic glass, under 2 mm in diameter, produced by explosive eruptions [1][2]. In skincare, volcanic ash, volcanic clay and related volcanic minerals appear as ingredients in some masks, cleansers and scrubs, especially in Korean-origin products that draw on Jeju Island's volcanic landscape [3][4]. Brands present them as oil-absorbing, pore-cleansing ingredients meant to leave skin looking less shiny and smoother.

The idea builds on a long history of using volcanic materials on skin. Pumice, a related light volcanic rock, has been used as an abrasive to remove dead skin and calluses since antiquity [5], and bentonite, a clay that usually forms when volcanic ash weathers, is widely used as an absorbent in cosmetics and dermatologic formulas [3].
Most of what is published about volcanic ash itself concerns geology and eruption hazards. No published clinical study has tested cosmetic volcanic ash on human skin.
infobox: Glass shards, mineral crystals, rock fragments [1]

paras: Volcanic ash consists of angular glass shards, crystals such as quartz, feldspar and pyroxene, and rock fragments. It is hard, abrasive and insoluble in water [1][2]. Colour ranges from light grey to black depending on the magma, and chemistry varies from silica-poor basaltic to silica-rich rhyolitic ash [1][2]. Fresh ash can carry soluble salts including chloride, sulfate and fluoride compounds that make it acidic when moist [1].

Ash is distinct from the soft residue of burnt wood or plants: it is made of hard rock-derived material with no organic component [2]. Because of that angularity and hardness, it has abrasive properties that cosmetic formulators can exploit in scrubs, while processed cosmetic grades are milled to controlled particle sizes.

sections.h: Related volcanic materials in personal care
paras: Bentonite is an absorbent, swelling clay made mostly of montmorillonite. Wikipedia states that it usually forms from the weathering of volcanic ash, and its large surface area and ion-exchange behaviour make it a strong adsorbent; it is used as a filler in cosmetics and as a base for many dermatologic formulas [3].

Pumice has been used on skin for thousands of years. Wikipedia describes its use in ancient Egypt to remove body hair, in ancient Rome in toothpastes, and in ancient China for nail grooming and callus removal; today it remains a common exfoliant in pedicures and in heavy-duty hand cleaners [5].

Korean beauty brands market several products built around Jeju volcanic ingredients. Innisfree, launched in 2000 by Amore Pacific, centres its concept on ingredients sourced from Jeju Island [4]. Product pages and reviews from brands describe volcanic clay or ash masks as pore-cleansing and sebum-absorbing; these are marketing descriptions, and Wikipedia's Innisfree article does not itself discuss volcanic masks [4].

Volcanology references describe inhaled eruption ash as causing respiratory, eye and skin irritation, mostly short-term; prolonged exposure to silica-rich ash carries a theoretical silicosis risk, though Wikipedia notes no documented silicosis cases from volcanic ash [1]. A 2026 review discusses how ash composition affects airway inflammation, immune modulation and infection risk [6]. These accounts concern eruption exposure rather than processed cosmetic ingredients.
As with other abrasive scrubs and drying clay masks, skin irritation is the most commonly expected effect of overuse; no specific adverse-event series for cosmetic volcanic ash has been published.

No studies found. Related literature concerns particulate toxicity in general: a review of nanomaterials discusses human exposure to natural particles such as volcanic ash [7], and laboratory studies of air-pollution particles examine inflammatory responses in lung cells [8]; these are not studies of cosmetic use.
